text: In eighteen ninety five, in a classroom in Calcutta, a teacher made a bell ring in another room. With no wire! He even set off a little gunpowder, right through two walls. His name was Jagadish Chandra Bose. And his trick is inside every radio. <#0.3#> Before that, sending a message far away needed a long, long wire. But there are invisible waves all around us. Like ripples in a pond, only you can't see them. <#0.3#> In eighteen sixty five, James Maxwell said these waves must exist. In eighteen eighty six, Heinrich Hertz made them with a spark. Bose made tiny waves, and sent them through two walls. Marconi filed his wireless patent in eighteen ninety six. In nineteen oh one, he said he heard a signal from across the ocean. <#0.3#> So how does a radio work? A tall metal rod at the radio station shakes tiny bits of electricity up and down, really fast. That makes invisible waves fly out, as fast as light. At your radio, the waves shake the tiny bits of electricity in its metal rod too. The radio turns that shaking into sound. <#0.3#> Every station sends a different wave. Turning the knob picks just one, like hearing one friend's voice in a noisy room. <#0.3#> Here's the surprise. Nobody invented radio alone. Maxwell, Hertz, Bose, Marconi and many others each added a piece, like a jigsaw puzzle. In India, the Radio Club of Bombay went on air in nineteen twenty three. All India Radio got its name in nineteen thirty six. Today, its signal reaches ninety nine in every hundred Indians. But only about five in a hundred homes still have a radio set. <#0.3#> Now you know.
